common_name: Variegated Mock Orange (White-Margined Sweet Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color is brightest and most stable with some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Site this variegated sport of the species sweet mock orange where its crisp white-margined foliage can be appreciated all season, since the leaf edging is the main ornamental draw and holds up better out of intense midday sun. The clean, cream-white leaf margins brighten shaded borders and pair well with dark-leaved companions long after the fleeting, sweetly fragrant white flowers of late spring have finished. Prune immediately after flowering to remove a portion of the oldest canes at the base each year, which keeps the shrub full and encourages strong new growth carrying the best variegation. Watch for occasional all-green reversion shoots and cut these out promptly at their point of origin to prevent them from overtaking the variegated growth.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; allow room for the gracefully arching branches to develop without crowding.

directions: This Lemoine-raised hybrid mock orange bears exceptionally large, single, pure-white flowers, each marked at the base with a distinct maroon-purple blotch that gives the blooms unusual depth and contrast against the arching branches in early summer. The fragrance is sweet and pronounced though somewhat lighter than that of the straight species, making it a fine choice near a patio or entry where the scent can be enjoyed without overwhelming the space. Prune immediately after flowering, thinning out a portion of the oldest wood at ground level each year to maintain the naturally graceful, fountain-like habit and promote strong new flowering canes. It tolerates a wide range of well-drained soils and, once established, needs only routine watering during extended dry spells.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent the cream-splashed foliage from scorching.

directions: Grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, this mock orange carries mid-green leaves irregularly splashed and blotched with cream and pale yellow, giving the whole shrub a bright, dappled look from spring through fall. In late spring it produces a generous crop of single, pure-white, sweetly fragrant flowers that stand out cleanly against the variegated backdrop. Prune immediately after flowering, cutting out some of the oldest stems at the base to keep growth vigorous and well furnished with the best-marked leaves. Cut out any shoots that revert to solid green as soon as they appear, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will gradually crowd out the variegated portions of the shrub.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in lean, sharply drained, even rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate considerable summer drought.

directions: Native to dry, rocky slopes and canyons across the southwestern United States, littleleaf mock orange is a compact, twiggy shrub with small gray-green leaves that punctuates its fine, drought-tolerant texture with a heavy crop of small, single, intensely sweet-scented white flowers in late spring to early summer. It is far more tolerant of heat, aridity, and lean, alkaline soils than the larger European and Pacific Northwest mock oranges, making it a good fit for xeric borders and rock gardens where a dependable fragrant shrub is otherwise hard to place. Prune lightly immediately after flowering only as needed to remove dead or crowded twiggy growth, since this species naturally holds a neat, dense form without heavy renewal pruning. Avoid rich soil and excess irrigation, both of which encourage lank growth and reduce the density and floral display that make this species valuable in dry gardens.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
